BEE 4750 Lab 2: Linear Programming with JuMP

Published

October 21, 2026

ImportantDue Date

Tuesday, October 27, 9:00pm

If you are enrolled in the course, make sure that you use the GitHub Classroom link provided in Ed Discussion, or you may not be able to get help if you run into problems.

Otherwise, you can find the Github repository here.

Setup

Run these two cells first. The first time, installing and loading JuMP and HiGHS can take a few minutes.

import Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.instantiate()
using JuMP    # optimization modeling syntax
using HiGHS   # the solver

Introduction

In the October 19 lecture, we saw how to formulate and solve a two-stack emissions problem in JuMP and read its shadow prices. In this lab you will do the same for three power plants on a hot summer afternoon: write its linear program in JuMP, solve it, read and interpret the shadow prices, and re-solve it when one limit tightens.

The Plants

A utility owns three power plants side by side on a river: a coal steam plant, a combined-cycle plant and a combustion-turbine plant. It sells all the electricity they generate at the wholesale price, $120/MWh this afternoon, and decides how much each plant should generate this hour to make the most profit. Each plant’s profit per MWh is the price minus its variable cost (mostly fuel).

Plant Capacity (MW) Variable cost ($/MWh) Heat to river (MWth per MW) NOx (lb/MWh)
Coal steam 600 30 1.5 1
Combined cycle 400 56 0.64 0.1
Combustion turbines 300 87 0 0.5

The three plants share three limits:

  • River heat. The coal plant and the combined-cycle plant are cooled with river water, which goes back into the river warmer. On a hot day the river is already warm, so the state caps the heat the three plants together may discharge to this stretch of the river: 1,000 MWth this hour. (MWth is megawatts of heat, to keep it apart from the MW of electricity the plants generate.) The combustion turbines are air-cooled and send no heat to the river.
  • NOx. Hot, sunny days are also ozone days, and NOx is one of the pollutants that forms ozone. Together, the three plants may emit at most 650 lb of NOx this hour.
  • Transmission line. The plants share one line to the grid, which can carry at most 1,000 MW.

The same data in code:

plant_names = ["Coal steam", "Combined cycle", "Combustion turbines"]
n_plants = length(plant_names)

price = 120                     # electricity price           [$/MWh]
variable_cost = [30, 56, 87]    # fuel and operating cost     [$/MWh]
capacity = [600, 400, 300]      # maximum output              [MW]
heat_to_river = [1.5, 0.64, 0]  # heat sent to the river      [MWth per MW]
nox_rate = [1, 0.1, 0.5]        # NOx emitted                 [lb/MWh]

heat_limit = 1000               # river heat permit           [MWth]
nox_limit = 650                 # NOx limit                   [lb]
line_limit = 1000               # transmission line capacity  [MW]

TipJuMP Syntax

From the October 19 lecture, a JuMP model has three kinds of pieces after the model itself:

model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
@variable(model, 0 <= amount[i in 1:n_items] <= upper_bound[i])
@objective(model, Max, sum(unit_value[i] * amount[i] for i in 1:n_items))
@constraint(model, budget,
    sum(unit_cost[i] * amount[i] for i in 1:n_items) <= available)

Use Max or Min as the problem needs. The name in @constraint (here budget) is how you ask about that constraint later. After optimize!(model):

  • value(amount[1]), or value.(amount) for all of them, gives the optimal decisions;
  • objective_value(model) gives the optimal objective;
  • value(budget) gives the constraint’s left-hand side at the optimum;
  • shadow_price(budget) gives the change in the objective when budget is relaxed by one unit.

Put the whole model in one cell and re-run that whole cell after any change. JuMP will not add a second constraint with the same name to a model, so re-running a single @constraint line gives an error.

Problem 1: Formulate the LP

Before writing any code, complete Problem 1 on the Activity Sheet: write the utility’s objective and the three shared limits as a linear program, with units. Use \(y_1\), \(y_2\) and \(y_3\) for the output of the coal plant, the combined-cycle plant and the combustion-turbine plant this hour, in MW. Each is at least 0 and at most its plant’s capacity.

Problem 2: Solve It in JuMP

Complete the model below from your Problem 1 formulation. The capacities are already in the @variable bounds. Write each of the three shared limits as a named constraint, using the names in the comments: the names are what let JuMP report their shadow prices in Problem 3.

utility = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
set_silent(utility)

# Output of each plant this hour [MW], between 0 and the plant's capacity
@variable(utility, 0 <= generation[i in 1:n_plants] <= capacity[i])

# TODO: the objective, the utility's profit this hour [$]
# @objective(utility, Max, ...)

# TODO: the three shared limits, each as a named constraint
# @constraint(utility, river_heat, ...)
# @constraint(utility, nox_emissions, ...)
# @constraint(utility, transmission_line, ...)

print(utility)

Check the printed model against your Activity Sheet, then solve it. The status should be OPTIMAL.

optimize!(utility)
termination_status(utility)
for i in 1:n_plants
    println(plant_names[i], ": ", value(generation[i]), " MW")
end
println("Profit: \$", objective_value(utility))

If your model matches the problem, the profit is $73,672 for the hour. If you get a different number, compare print(utility) with your Problem 1 formulation, or ask the TA.

How much of each limit does this plan use?

println("River heat: ", value(river_heat), " of ", heat_limit, " MWth")
println("NOx: ", value(nox_emissions), " of ", nox_limit, " lb")
println("Line: ", value(transmission_line), " of ", line_limit, " MW")

Problem 3: Shadow Prices

Use shadow_price to get the shadow price of each of the three named constraints.

# TODO: the shadow price of each named constraint, for example
# println("River heat: ", shadow_price(river_heat))

JuMP’s shadow_price is the change in the objective when a constraint is relaxed by one unit. This model maximizes profit, and relaxing a limit can only raise the best profit or leave it unchanged, so expect shadow prices that are positive or zero. (In the cost-minimizing emissions problem from lecture they were negative or zero, for the same reason.)

Complete Problem 3 on the Activity Sheet.

Problem 4: A Hotter River

The heat wave deepens: the river warms further, and the state cuts the plants’ heat limit from 1,000 to 850 MWth. Answer Problem 4a on the Activity Sheet, a prediction from the shadow price, before you re-solve.

First, save the results under the current limit, since re-solving will replace them:

base_generation = value.(generation)
base_profit = objective_value(utility)
base_nox = value(nox_emissions)

Now lower the heat limit and solve again. set_normalized_rhs changes a constraint’s right-hand side in the model you already built, as in the October 19 lecture.

heatwave_heat_limit = 850   # [MWth]

# TODO: lower the river heat limit to heatwave_heat_limit, then solve again
# set_normalized_rhs(river_heat, ...)
# optimize!(utility)
for i in 1:n_plants
    println(plant_names[i], ": ", base_generation[i], " MW before, ",
        value(generation[i]), " MW after")
end
println("Profit: \$", base_profit, " before, \$",
    objective_value(utility), " after")
println("NOx: ", base_nox, " lb before, ", value(nox_emissions), " lb after")
